subject: An IT Question:  Running Stan on massively parallel platforms

messages.author: 14c3a76cbb24a2d2
messages.subject: An IT Question:  Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts: One can read that Stan is supported on multiple laptops but what about parallel platforms?  For instance if I have access to a cluster on Amazon's S3 cloud, Hadoop, Netezza or any massively parallel cluster somewhere, will Stan run?  If so, is there anything different that one should know about setting Stan up in one of these environments?  Or is it just plug and play?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts:
Assuming that you're referring only to running Stan within an instance of one of these clusters (as opposed to having a cluster farm out calculations internal to Stan which is not possible at the moment)
then the answer is it depends on your environment.  The requirements for Stan (and whichever interface you're using) are listed in the manual and provided you can configure the local environment
appropriate then Stan should have no problem running.  For example, Stan runs entirely locally and doesn't require the ability to read/write anywhere external.

I have multiple colleagues who have gotten Stan running on clusters once the environment was configured correctly and something like S3 should be no problem once you set up the VM appropriately.
On Wed, Sep 24, 2014 at 11:10 AM, Thomas Ball <xtc...@gmail.com> wrote:

One can read that Stan is supported on multiple laptops but what about parallel platforms?  For instance if I have access to a cluster on Amazon's S3 cloud, Hadoop, Netezza or any massively parallel cluster somewhere, will Stan run?  If so, is there anything different that one should know about setting Stan up in one of these environments?  Or is it just plug and play?

messages.author: 14c3a76cbb24a2d2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts:
Michael-

    Thank you.  That sounds like it might be good news regarding Stan and MPPs.  As with everything though, the devil's always in the details.  So, you write of running Stan "within an instance of one of these clusters."  Does this mean that if there are 100, 1,000 or more CPUs in a cluster that Stan can leverage an "instance," i.e., a single CPU?  If this is true, and I think you're saying this, Stan is not currently able to leverage the full distributed processing power in the cluster.   It would, however, be able to exploit the significantly greater (vs laptop) memory and storage capacity typically available in one of these environments.

   Next, the provision for "configuring the local environment" sounds like you're giving someone enough rope to hang themselves -- and I do not mean to be snide here.  Could you provide guidance or be more specific about what this entails?  As we know, Stan is pretty much plug and play on laptops.  Do you have to be a Cloudera expert, a Hadoop manager, or a computer scientist to "configure the local environment" as you put it in an MPP to enable Stan to compile?  If I'm none of these things and am little more than a hapless user who knows enough background IT to get some analysis done, am I basically screwed?  Or, worse, would I have to pay a consultant hundreds, if not thousands of dollars to "configure the local environment?"  

    Depending on how these questions or concerns get answered, Stan will be more or less viable on an MPP.

Thank you again!

messages.author: 275b133a3506805a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts:
Thomas,

Just a user here: Stan doesn't have parallellisation "inside", as
Michael said, so for parallel processing the approach is the simple
one of running multiple completely separate stan processes and
combining the outputs. See "Sampling in Parallel" in the cmdstan
manual (not the main stan manual, the cmdstan manual). They show
examples of running multiple processes, each with their own chain-id,
and a common random seed. This approach should be OK for
massively-parallel setups, though I haven't tried it. Stan works fine
on standard debian/ubuntu so I'd be surprised if you have to do any
difficult config on a cloud system such as amazon's.

Best
Dan

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts:
Let me first say that there will not be one "answer", nor is there rarely such a concept when talking about clusters whose architectures can vary widely.
This kind of problem is not related to Stan but rather the architecture and administration of the problem at hand.

Firstly, at the moment Stan is single-threaded and entirely serial.  If you have multiple cores, whether they are cores on a single chip or cores in a large
cluster, then Stan can run on one and only one of them.  Just like any other serial process.

So if you want to run Stan with a billion data points within a single model then a cluster isn't going to help you (nor should it -- this is a deeper statistical 
question that's best left for another thread).  But if you wanted to run multiple models or multiple chains, then a cluster might be of use.  In this case
the only question is whether or not the cluster meets the Stan dependencies.

If the cluster runs off a (presumably Linux-based) virtual machine then there's no problem.  You can configure the VM to grab Eigen and Boost and the 
latest compiler and Stan will run locally in the VM without any issue.

If the cluster runs off a local environment then you have to ensure that he cluster admins install the necessary components for you (or give you the
permissions to do it yourself).  This can be easy or a pain, depending on how these kinds of requests are managed at a particular cluster.  But, again,
not something particular to Stan.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts:
We don't provide any out-of-the-box configurations for clusters
with Stan. We've run Stan on clusters for experiments where we
want to deal with multiple parameterizatons, models, etc. It requires
some basic cluster-specific config.

There's always an issue with configuring the local environments on
clusters. Something like Amazon's EC2 lets you do that in a brute
force way by effectively taking a snapshot of an entire OS and then
running multiple instances of it.

Stan may be integrated into Shogun relatively soon (don't know what
their schedule or commitment level is), which may provide some hooks
to some clusters.

Given that you haven't said what problem you're trying to solve
and what hardware you have, it's impossible provide specific
suggestions.

- Bob

parts:
You're not really going to be able to use Stan to build
random forests. It involves discrete non-parametric
components we can't sample over.

There's BART --- the Bayesian additive regression tree
package in R, but I don't know how possible it would be to
parallelize.

- Bob

messages.author: 14c3a76cbb24a2d2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] An IT Question: Running Stan on massively parallel platforms
parts:
Hi Bob-
   Thanks for your observation.  The caveat is duly noted.  Dan's proposed a simple, brute force workaround that involves loading Stan across all of the available CPUs, running chains or ensembles of models, then rolling them all up at the end.  That's very practical and is in the spirit if not the letter of Cleveland's D&R approach.  Big data shops in the applied world are doing this, running millions of mini-models in a few hours on an MPP, then aggregating it all at the end to produce an approximate model.  I've also heard about a Bayesian vendor doing the same, generating billions of parameters in the process.  Brave new world it is.
Tom
